_comment: Rotating content bank. The script picks items deterministically by date so each day's edition is different. Edit freely — just keep the shape.

newsbrief.lead: Brits now spend an average of 14 hours a week on streaming — more than cooking, cleaning and exercising combined.
newsbrief.detail: The biggest jump is in the over-55s, who used to be the holdouts for live telly. 'Second-screening' means we pay less attention than ever.

newsbrief.lead: 62% of us have lied about reading a book to look smart in front of someone we fancy.
newsbrief.detail: Most-faked titles: 1984, Pride and Prejudice and (awkwardly) the Bible. One in five admit to faking a whole dinner-party conversation about a novel they'd only seen the cover of.

newsbrief.lead: Holiday firms report a 40% spike in 'shoulder season' bookings — September and October sun trips are way up on last year.
newsbrief.detail: Travellers blame school-holiday flight prices, unreliable summer weather, and 'August feels too crowded these days'. Spain, Greece and Portugal top the wish list.

newsbrief.lead: More than half of UK workers would take a 10% pay cut to never go into the office again — but only 17% of bosses say they'd offer one.
newsbrief.detail: The gap is growing again after forced return-to-office rules. HR experts say the tension shows up in resignation rates, particularly for under-35s.

newsbrief.lead: Three quarters of dog owners now talk to their dog more than they talk to their partner.
newsbrief.detail: Top topics: 'what we're doing later', 'what we just saw out the window' and a surprising amount of Bake Off commentary. 12% admit they've apologised to the dog after a row with the human.

newsbrief.lead: Britain's most-stolen supermarket item in 2026 isn't meat or cheese — it's olive oil, with theft up 220% year on year.
newsbrief.detail: Prices have nearly doubled in two years. Some shops have fitted security tags to single bottles, others have moved premium brands behind the counter — like cigarettes.

newsbrief.lead: The fastest-growing hobby of 2026 is hand-embroidery — sales of needles and thread up 180% in a year.
newsbrief.detail: Crafters say it's the perfect 'phone detox' — slow, tactile, satisfying. TikTok is full of 20-somethings showing off custom denim jackets.

newsbrief.lead: Almost two thirds of us say we've cried at a podcast in the last year — grief, parenting and identity top the list of triggers.
newsbrief.detail: Researchers reckon it's the intimacy of audio that does it. The figure is even higher for under-30s, 71% of whom admit a recent podcast-induced tear.

newsbrief.lead: Half of UK adults can't name a single member of the cabinet — but 80% can name three Love Island contestants.
newsbrief.detail: Political engagement researchers say it's not apathy so much as 'noise overload'. People remember faces from things they actively watch.

newsbrief.lead: The most-Googled DIY question in Britain this year: 'how to remove silicone'.
newsbrief.detail: Tradespeople say it's the rise of botched bathroom resealing jobs during lockdown that's still haunting people. YouTube tutorials on the topic have racked up 60 million views.

newsbrief.lead: One in three of us has had a 'sleep divorce' — sleeping in a separate bed from our partner.
newsbrief.detail: Reasons: snoring (45%), different schedules (30%), restless legs, and one bizarre 12% who say their partner 'talks to the cat in their sleep'.

newsbrief.lead: British baby names are getting shorter again — three- and four-letter names are dominating the registrar.
newsbrief.detail: Top picks this year: Noa, Ezra, Ada and Bo. Long, multi-syllable Victorian names like Theodora are sliding back down the chart.

newsbrief.lead: The average Brit checks their phone 159 times a day — but says it 'doesn't feel like that much'.
newsbrief.detail: Researchers using passive monitoring apps say we badly underestimate our own usage. Most people guess between 30 and 70 times.

newsbrief.lead: Cash is making a small comeback — ATM withdrawals are up 14% on this time last year.
newsbrief.detail: Bank analysts credit budget-conscious households using cash to stay disciplined. The 'envelope method' is back trending on TikTok.

newsbrief.lead: Roses are out, peonies are in — UK florists report a 200% rise in peony orders for weddings this summer.
newsbrief.detail: Brides cite 'softer, less staged' aesthetics. Wholesale peony prices have crept up accordingly.

newsbrief.lead: Pubs report a Tuesday boom — the new 'mid-week meet' is the fastest-growing dining occasion.
newsbrief.detail: Operators say WFH-ers like getting out the house mid-week without the weekend crowds. Tuesday wine sales are up almost 30%.

newsbrief.lead: Loneliness is now considered a bigger health risk than smoking 15 cigarettes a day, according to NHS England.
newsbrief.detail: Social prescribing — GPs referring patients to community activities — is rolling out nationwide. Walking groups, book clubs and choirs are reportedly oversubscribed.

newsbrief.lead: Almost 70% of UK households now have a smart speaker — but the most common use is still 'asking what time it is'.
newsbrief.detail: Researchers say we under-use the devices we own. Setting timers, playing music and weather queries make up two thirds of all commands.

newsbrief.lead: The 'silver gamer' is the fastest-growing demographic in UK gaming — over-65s spent £180 million on games last year.
newsbrief.detail: Cosy life-sim titles like Stardew Valley and Animal Crossing dominate. Console makers are reportedly designing larger UI for the market.

newsbrief.lead: Brits spend an average of 38 minutes a day deciding what to watch — and 12 of those are spent scrolling Netflix.
newsbrief.detail: 'Watch-paralysis' has its own subreddit. Streamers are quietly experimenting with 'shuffle' buttons that just play something.

newsbrief.lead: Brits are apparently buying more houseplants than ever — and naming them.
newsbrief.detail: A garden survey found nearly a third of plant owners have given their plants names, and a surprising number apologise to them when they forget to water.

newsbrief.lead: The humble flask is having a comeback, with sales up sharply as people try to cut café spending.
newsbrief.detail: Retailers say the big winner is the 'keeps drinks hot for 12 hours' bottle — though most of us still drink it within the first one.

newsbrief.lead: A study says the average person walks past their phone over 50 times a day without picking it up.
newsbrief.detail: Researchers reckon just seeing it nearby is enough reassurance. The phone, meanwhile, remains entirely unbothered.

newsbrief.lead: Allotment waiting lists have hit record highs across the UK.
newsbrief.detail: Councils in some areas now quote waits of several years. The most-grown first crop for beginners? Courgettes — closely followed by regret, as they produce far too many.

newsbrief.lead: More of us are taking up 'fake commutes' — a short walk before and after working from home.
newsbrief.detail: Psychologists say the made-up journey helps separate work from home life. Some people even pop to a shop and back to 'arrive'.

newsbrief.lead: Board game cafés are booming on UK high streets.
newsbrief.detail: Owners say the biggest sellers are the quick, daft games — not the four-hour epics. The most common cause of fallouts remains the rules of a certain word game.

newsbrief.lead: A survey finds most of us have at least one app we've never opened since downloading it.
newsbrief.detail: The average phone reportedly carries dozens of unused apps. Top of the 'meant to use it' pile: language-learning and meditation.

newsbrief.lead: Tinned fish is unexpectedly trendy again, with younger shoppers leading the charge.
newsbrief.detail: Sardines and mackerel are being repackaged as a quick, cheap protein. Older shoppers are quietly baffled, having eaten it for decades.

newsbrief.lead: Britain's appetite for 'cosy' nights in is reshaping Friday nights.
newsbrief.detail: Takeaway and streaming bookings now peak earlier in the evening, as more of us swap the big night out for a big night in.

newsbrief.lead: The number of people learning to play an instrument as an adult is rising fast.
newsbrief.detail: Piano and guitar lead the way, with online lessons making it easier. The hardest part, learners say, is finding somewhere to practise without an audience.

newsbrief.lead: A poll says most people can't remember the last time they wrote a letter by hand.
newsbrief.detail: Yet greetings-card sales remain strong — we'll happily sign our name, just not write a full page.

newsbrief.lead: 'Quiet' holidays are the new luxury, with travellers seeking places with nothing much to do.
newsbrief.detail: Tour operators report rising demand for remote cottages and slow trains. The number one requested feature: a reliable kettle and a view.

newsbrief.lead: Reusable coffee cups are finally outnumbering disposables in some city centres.
newsbrief.detail: Cafés offering a small discount have seen the biggest shift. The catch: most of us still leave the cup at home half the time.

newsbrief.lead: More households are growing herbs on the windowsill to cut grocery bills.
newsbrief.detail: Basil and mint are the favourites. Survival rates, gardeners admit, are 'mixed' — the basil rarely makes it past a fortnight.

newsbrief.lead: A study suggests we underestimate how much our neighbours would like to be asked for help.
newsbrief.detail: Researchers say a small favour often builds friendships faster than years of polite nodding over the fence.

newsbrief.lead: Swimming in the sea and lakes — 'wild swimming' — keeps growing in popularity year-round.
newsbrief.detail: Enthusiasts swear by the cold-water buzz. Newcomers are advised to start gently, and that the gasp on entry is completely normal.

newsbrief.lead: The crossword and puzzle boom is still going strong, in print and on phones.
newsbrief.detail: Publishers report a surge in daily puzzlers. The most argued-over answer in households remains anything involving a cryptic clue.

newsbrief.lead: Slow cookers are flying off the shelves again as energy-conscious shoppers rediscover them.
newsbrief.detail: They use a fraction of the power of an oven over a day. The downside: the smell of dinner from 9am tests everyone's patience.

newsbrief.lead: A survey says most of us have a 'signature dish' we bring out whenever guests come round.
newsbrief.detail: Chilli, lasagne and a roast top the list. Very few of us, it turns out, have a second dish ready if the first goes wrong.

newsbrief.lead: Local 'repair cafés', where volunteers fix broken items for free, are spreading across the UK.
newsbrief.detail: Toasters, lamps and zips are the most common patients. Organisers say the biggest barrier is convincing people their old kettle is worth saving.

newsbrief.lead: More people are switching their morning scroll for a morning walk, apps suggest.
newsbrief.detail: Step-counters report a small but steady rise in early-morning activity. The motivation for most? A dog that refuses to wait.

newsbrief.lead: Charity shops are reporting a surge in both donations and shoppers as 'pre-loved' goes mainstream.
newsbrief.detail: Younger shoppers in particular are hunting for one-off finds. Volunteers say the most donated item by a mile is the unworn 'someday' outfit.

newsbrief.lead: A study finds the average person has a 'comfort route' they walk or drive even when there's a faster way.
newsbrief.detail: Familiarity, not speed, wins. We'd rather the known road with the nice tree than save three minutes on the ring road.

newsbrief.lead: Jigsaw puzzles are still selling in huge numbers, years after their lockdown boom.
newsbrief.detail: 1,000-piece designs are the sweet spot. The most dreaded puzzle remains anything that's mostly sky.

newsbrief.lead: Britons are keeping their phones for longer than ever before upgrading.
newsbrief.detail: The average handset is now held onto for several years. The main reason cited isn't loyalty — it's the dread of moving everything across.

newsbrief.lead: A survey says most of us secretly prefer a night in with a quiz on the telly to a night out.
newsbrief.detail: Shouting answers at the screen remains the nation's favourite low-effort sport — even when we're completely wrong.

newsbrief.lead: Community 'little libraries' — swap-a-book boxes on the street — are popping up in more neighbourhoods.
newsbrief.detail: The unwritten rule is take one, leave one. The most-swapped genre, organisers say, is the holiday thriller.

newsbrief.lead: More of us are batch-cooking at the weekend to dodge the weeknight scramble.
newsbrief.detail: Freezers are filling with portioned dinners. The classic mistake: forgetting to label them, then playing 'mystery soup' on a Wednesday.

newsbrief.lead: A poll finds the nation can't agree on the correct way to make a cup of tea.
newsbrief.detail: Milk first or last remains a genuine source of household tension. The one thing we agree on: someone else should make it.

newsbrief.lead: Pub quizzes are reporting record team sign-ups, with niche rounds drawing the crowds.
newsbrief.detail: Music and picture rounds are the great levellers. The cleverest team name still wins more goodwill than the actual answers.

newsbrief.lead: Cold-water taps for filling pets' bowls and watering cans are the surprise garden-centre hit.
newsbrief.detail: With more of us gardening, small convenience gadgets are booming — though the watering can remains undefeated.

newsbrief.lead: A study suggests humming or singing badly in the car genuinely lifts your mood.
newsbrief.detail: Researchers link it to deep breathing and a small dose of joy. Fellow drivers at the lights may not share the enthusiasm.

newsbrief.lead: More people are writing 'done lists' instead of to-do lists to feel better about their day.
newsbrief.detail: Noting what you actually achieved, however small, apparently beats staring at everything you didn't. 'Got dressed' counts.

newsbrief.lead: The great British picnic is being upgraded, with sales of fold-out chairs and cool bags climbing.
newsbrief.detail: We're venturing out more, weather permitting. The traditional picnic still ends, as ever, with at least one item dropped in the grass.

newsbrief.lead: A survey finds most of us have a drawer, shelf or cupboard we're slightly afraid to open.
newsbrief.detail: The 'everything drawer' is a near-universal feature of British homes. Inside: takeaway menus, dead batteries and one very important thing we'll never find again.

newsbrief.lead: Cycling to the shops is up, with more people using bikes for short local trips rather than big rides.
newsbrief.detail: Councils credit better cycle lanes. The number one cargo carried? A surprisingly heavy single bag for life.

newsbrief.lead: More of us are learning the names of the birds in our gardens, apps report.
newsbrief.detail: Bird-ID apps have made spotting easier. The robin remains the nation's clear favourite, mostly for its cheek.

newsbrief.lead: A study says the smell of fresh bread is one of the few things almost everyone finds comforting.
newsbrief.detail: Supermarkets have long known it — the in-store bakery is no accident. Few of us escape without an unplanned loaf.

newsbrief.lead: Knitting and crochet are booming with a new generation, sold as the ultimate screen-free wind-down.
newsbrief.detail: Beginners start with scarves and quietly accumulate wool. The first project, makers admit, is usually 'a bit wonky but loved'.

newsbrief.lead: A poll finds most people have a song that instantly makes them feel like dancing, even in the kitchen.
newsbrief.detail: Kitchen discos are a quiet national pastime. The wooden spoon remains the microphone of choice.

survey.question: 71% of us admit to doing THIS in the car when we think no-one is watching. What is it?
survey.answer: singing at the top of our lungs, with full dramatic facial expressions.

survey.question: Asked 'what's the most British thing about your morning?', the number one answer wasn't a cup of tea — it was THIS.
survey.answer: apologising to someone who walked into you.

survey.question: 48% of us do THIS every single day. What is it?
survey.answer: step on the bathroom scales.

survey.question: 63% of us have done THIS in a meeting we're meant to be paying attention to. What?
survey.answer: online shopping.

survey.question: 82% of us secretly enjoy doing THIS, even though we'd never admit it. What?
survey.answer: watching neighbours through the curtains.

survey.question: When asked what they'd grab in a house fire after their pets and family, 40% said THIS. What?
survey.answer: the phone charger.

survey.question: 57% of UK workers admit doing THIS while on a work call. What?
survey.answer: going to the loo.

survey.question: Asked what makes them feel old, the top answer wasn't grey hairs — it was THIS. What?
survey.answer: not recognising any of the names at the top of the charts.

survey.question: 44% of us have done THIS while waiting for a kettle to boil. What?
survey.answer: wandered off and forgotten about it entirely.

survey.question: 75% of us check THIS more than ten times a day. What?
survey.answer: the weather app.

survey.question: 61% of us have lied about THIS to get out of a social event. What?
survey.answer: having a cold.

survey.question: 53% of people admit to doing THIS in a restaurant when no-one's looking. What?
survey.answer: licking the plate.

survey.question: 69% of Brits do THIS as soon as they get in from work. What?
survey.answer: take their trousers off and put pyjama bottoms on.

survey.question: 39% of us have done THIS in a supermarket trolley aisle. What?
survey.answer: had a full domestic argument.

survey.question: 68% of us admit to keeping THIS for years even though it doesn't work. What is it?
survey.answer: a pen we know is dead, that we put back in the drawer anyway.

survey.question: Asked the most pointless thing they do every day, Brits' number one answer was THIS.
survey.answer: checking the fridge again, hoping new food has appeared.

survey.question: Nearly 6 in 10 of us have a 'special' version of THIS we won't let anyone else use.
survey.answer: a favourite mug.

survey.question: Asked what instantly makes a hotel feel posh, the top answer wasn't the pool — it was THIS.
survey.answer: a little tray of free biscuits.

survey.question: 74% of us have done THIS to avoid talking to someone we know in a supermarket.
survey.answer: pretended to be fascinated by a shelf of beans.

survey.question: The most common thing we say we'll 'start on Monday' is THIS.
survey.answer: the diet — again.

survey.question: 63% of dog owners admit they've done THIS when no-one's around.
survey.answer: had a full conversation with the dog about their day.

survey.question: Asked the most British way to end a phone call, the winner was THIS string of words.
survey.answer: 'right… okay then… lovely… bye, bye, bye, bye.'

survey.question: Over half of us confess we've kept THIS appliance long after it broke 'just in case'.
survey.answer: a toaster that only does one side.

survey.question: The number one thing we pretend to understand but don't is THIS.
survey.answer: how our own pension works.

survey.question: 61% of us have a drawer at home that contains mostly THIS.
survey.answer: random cables we'll never identify again.

survey.question: Asked the food we'd happily eat cold straight from the fridge, the top answer was THIS.
survey.answer: last night's leftover pizza.

survey.question: 7 in 10 of us have lied about THIS to get off the phone faster.
survey.answer: 'oh, you're breaking up, I'm going into a tunnel.'

survey.question: The most common thing we Google late at night is apparently THIS.
survey.answer: whether it's normal that our knee just did that.

survey.question: 58% of us admit we judge a person instantly based on THIS.
survey.answer: how they treat waiting staff.

survey.question: Asked the most satisfying household sound, the winner was THIS.
survey.answer: the click of the kettle as it finishes boiling.

survey.question: Two-thirds of us have pretended to like THIS to be polite.
survey.answer: a friend's questionable home cooking.

survey.question: The thing we most often put off until 'tomorrow' is THIS.
survey.answer: sorting out the photos on our phone.

survey.question: 65% of us still do THIS even though every map app exists.
survey.answer: ask a stranger for directions and then immediately ignore them.

survey.question: Asked what's in the bottom of nearly every handbag, the top answer was THIS.
survey.answer: a single mysterious receipt from 2019.

survey.question: Over 70% of us admit we've rewatched THIS rather than try something new.
survey.answer: the same comfort show for the hundredth time.

survey.question: The most common reason we open the fridge is apparently NOT hunger — it's THIS.
survey.answer: boredom.

survey.question: 59% of us have a name for THIS that only our family understands.
survey.answer: the remote control — ours is apparently called all sorts.

survey.question: Asked the most stressful part of a group meal out, the top answer was THIS.
survey.answer: working out how to split the bill.

survey.question: 64% of us keep THIS even though we've never once read it.
survey.answer: the instruction manual for the microwave.

survey.question: The thing we most often say we 'don't really watch' but absolutely do is THIS.
survey.answer: reality TV.

survey.question: Just over half of us admit to doing THIS with the TV remote.
survey.answer: hiding it so someone else can't change the channel.

survey.question: Asked the smell that instantly takes us back to childhood, the winner was THIS.
survey.answer: cut grass on a summer afternoon.

survey.question: 66% of us have pretended to be busy to avoid THIS.
survey.answer: helping someone move house.

survey.question: The most common thing we forget the moment we walk into a room is THIS.
survey.answer: why we walked into the room.

survey.question: 60% of us have a 'good' version of THIS we save for visitors.
survey.answer: the nice towels nobody's allowed to actually use.

survey.question: Asked the most annoying noise in everyday life, the top answer was THIS.
survey.answer: someone else's phone on full volume on the train.

survey.question: 57% of us admit we've bought THIS purely because it was on offer.
survey.answer: something we had absolutely no use for.

survey.question: The thing we're most likely to lie about our skill at is THIS.
survey.answer: parallel parking.

survey.question: 69% of us do THIS the moment we get into a hotel room.
survey.answer: check behind the bathroom door and test every light switch.

survey.question: Asked the most British weather complaint, the winner was THIS.
survey.answer: 'it's not the heat, it's the humidity.'

survey.question: Over half of us confess we've kept a gift we hated because of THIS.
survey.answer: guilt that the giver might visit and notice it's gone.

survey.question: The most common thing we do in a lift is apparently THIS.
survey.answer: stare at the numbers as if they're enthralling.

survey.question: 62% of us have a particular THIS we refuse to throw away.
survey.answer: a battered old hoodie that's basically held together by memories.

survey.question: Asked what we'd grab first if we had ten seconds to leave the house, the top answer was THIS.
survey.answer: the phone — obviously.

survey.question: 71% of us judge a cafe instantly on THIS.
survey.answer: whether the toilets are nice.

survey.question: The most common little victory that makes our whole day is apparently THIS.
survey.answer: getting the green light all the way to work.

talk_topic.lead: A new study says we form a strong opinion of someone within 7 seconds of meeting them.
talk_topic.detail: Talk-back: what's the quickest you've ever decided you didn't like someone — and were you right? Or the quickest you DID like someone?

talk_topic.lead: Matching pet-and-owner outfits are apparently making a comeback this summer.
talk_topic.detail: Would you actually do it? And if so — does the dog get a vote in the wardrobe?

talk_topic.lead: If you could only listen to one song for the rest of your life, what is it?
talk_topic.detail: Talk-back: pick one. No 'depends on the mood'. Just one song forever — go.

talk_topic.lead: What's the most British thing you've ever done?
talk_topic.detail: Talk-back: bonus points for the apology, the queue and the cup of tea all in one anecdote.

talk_topic.lead: A survey says 30% of us have a 'forever favourite' meal we'd be happy eating every day.
talk_topic.detail: Talk-back: what's yours? And could you really eat it every day?

talk_topic.lead: Researchers say the average person has 27 unread voicemails. We're voicemail-phobic.
talk_topic.detail: Talk-back: when did you last actually listen to one? And who left it?

talk_topic.lead: If you won the lottery tonight, what's the FIRST thing you'd buy tomorrow?
talk_topic.detail: Talk-back: not the dream house. Not the holiday. The first daft thing you'd buy because you finally could.

talk_topic.lead: What's the worst job you've ever had — and how long did you last?
talk_topic.detail: Talk-back: the war stories are usually the funniest. Bonus marks for under a fortnight.

talk_topic.lead: A study claims our taste in music is 'locked in' by age 14.
talk_topic.detail: Talk-back: do you still listen to what you loved at 14? And what was on your bedroom wall?

talk_topic.lead: What's the most embarrassing thing in your kitchen that you'd hide if guests came round?
talk_topic.detail: Talk-back: bonus marks for anyone admitting to a Slap Chop or a NutriBullet bought once and never used.

talk_topic.lead: Apparently 1 in 5 of us have a 'comfort show' we've watched more than 10 times.
talk_topic.detail: Talk-back: what's yours? Friends? Gavin and Stacey? Bake Off? Reveal yourself.

talk_topic.lead: If you could un-invent ONE thing from modern life, what would it be?
talk_topic.detail: Talk-back: not phones. Pick something specific. Self-checkouts? Wireless earbuds that always die? The Selfridges Christmas advert?

talk_topic.lead: Researchers say the most stressful day to drive in the UK isn't Monday — it's THIS day.
talk_topic.detail: (Spoiler: it's Thursday.) Talk-back: what day of the week feels longest to you, and why?

talk_topic.lead: The 'big shop' is dying — younger Brits are doing 4–6 small shops a week instead.
talk_topic.detail: Talk-back: are you a one-big-shop person or a daily-corner-shop person? And which one is your partner?

talk_topic.lead: A new survey says the average person has three 'comfort meals' they return to again and again.
talk_topic.detail: Talk-back: what are yours — and is there one you'd genuinely be happy to eat every single day?

talk_topic.lead: Apparently most of us still have a landline number memorised from childhood.
talk_topic.detail: Whose number can you still recite by heart — and could you remember your own mobile if you tried?

talk_topic.lead: Researchers reckon the perfect length for a nap is 26 minutes.
talk_topic.detail: Are you a napper or does it ruin your whole night? And what's the worst place you've ever fallen asleep?

talk_topic.lead: A study claims the song you loved at 14 is the one you'll love forever.
talk_topic.detail: What was yours — and are you brave enough to admit it on air?

talk_topic.lead: Most people apparently have one job they wanted as a child and completely abandoned.
talk_topic.detail: What did you want to be? And how far did real life take you from it?

talk_topic.lead: New research says we're at our most creative in the shower.
talk_topic.detail: What's the best idea you've ever had standing under the water — and did you actually do anything with it?

talk_topic.lead: Apparently the average household argues most about the thermostat.
talk_topic.detail: Who controls the heating in your house — and has it ever started a proper row?

talk_topic.lead: A survey says most of us have a 'forbidden' word we can't stand.
talk_topic.detail: What's the word that makes your skin crawl? Go on, share it.

talk_topic.lead: Scientists say humans can recognise a friend just from the sound of them walking.
talk_topic.detail: Who can you identify by their footsteps alone — and has anyone ever crept up and caught you out?

talk_topic.lead: A new poll says the most-missed shop from the high street is one a lot of us took for granted.
talk_topic.detail: Which closed-down shop do you still think about — and what did you always buy there?

talk_topic.lead: Most of us apparently have one recipe we've made so often we could do it blindfolded.
talk_topic.detail: What's your signature dish — and where did you learn it?

talk_topic.lead: Researchers say the smell of a particular food can transport you straight back decades.
talk_topic.detail: What smell instantly takes you back — and to exactly where?

talk_topic.lead: A study claims we all have one chore we secretly enjoy.
talk_topic.detail: Which household job do you actually find satisfying — and which one would you happily never do again?

talk_topic.lead: Apparently most people have a 'lucky' item they take to big occasions.
talk_topic.detail: What's yours — and has it ever actually worked?

talk_topic.lead: New research says the average person has visited fewer than half the places on their own doorstep.
talk_topic.detail: What's the famous local spot you've still never been to despite living nearby for years?

talk_topic.lead: A survey says most of us would fail a test on the rules of a sport we watch every week.
talk_topic.detail: Which sport do you love but couldn't actually explain the rules of?

talk_topic.lead: Apparently we all have a phrase a parent or grandparent said that we now catch ourselves saying.
talk_topic.detail: What's the saying you swore you'd never repeat — and now say constantly?

talk_topic.lead: Scientists reckon the best cure for a bad mood is a ten-minute walk.
talk_topic.detail: What's your go-to reset when the day's gone wrong — a walk, a brew, a particular song?

talk_topic.lead: A new study says most people keep a ticket, photo or trinket from a day that changed their life.
talk_topic.detail: What's the keepsake you'll never throw away — and what's the story behind it?

talk_topic.lead: Apparently the average person has one skill that always impresses people.
talk_topic.detail: What's your party trick — and when did you discover you could do it?

talk_topic.lead: Researchers say the average commute is the time we do our best thinking.
talk_topic.detail: What have you decided, planned or solved on the way to work?

talk_topic.lead: A poll says most of us have a film we'll stop and watch no matter what part it's at.
talk_topic.detail: Which film reels you in every single time it's on?

talk_topic.lead: Apparently we all have one word we can never spell right first time.
talk_topic.detail: What's the word that defeats you — even with autocorrect?

talk_topic.lead: New research suggests the happiest people have a 'small ritual' that starts their day.
talk_topic.detail: What's the little thing you do every morning that sets you up — and what happens if you skip it?

talk_topic.lead: A survey says most of us have given a nickname to a stranger we see regularly.
talk_topic.detail: Who's the person on your route you've secretly named — and what did you call them?

talk_topic.lead: Apparently the average person changes their mind about their favourite biscuit three times in a lifetime.
talk_topic.detail: What's your current number one — and what's it knocked off the top spot?

talk_topic.lead: Scientists say a good laugh is as good for your heart as light exercise.
talk_topic.detail: Who in your life can make you laugh no matter what — and what's the daftest thing that's set you off?

talk_topic.lead: A new study says most people have a 'comfort programme' they put on to fall asleep.
talk_topic.detail: What do you drift off to — and does your other half agree with the choice?

talk_topic.lead: Apparently most of us have one thing we collect without ever meaning to.
talk_topic.detail: What have you somehow ended up with dozens of — tote bags, mugs, odd socks?

talk_topic.lead: Researchers reckon the average person has a 'go-to' story they tell at every party.
talk_topic.detail: What's the tale you always wheel out — and is it even still true?

true_false.fact: A council in the North-West has agreed to fix a much-complained-about pothole only after a resident planted a small tree in it and the photo went viral. The pothole had been reported 17 times in a year before the tree solved it overnight.
true_false.fiction: A Devon village has voted unanimously to ban Vinted couriers from parking on its narrow high street, after a single delivery driver knocked over the same pub's hanging basket three weeks in a row.

true_false.fact: A Yorkshire farmer has won a planning row by getting his prize-winning sheep listed as 'agricultural heritage', preventing a housing development from going ahead next to his field.
true_false.fiction: A Cornish café has started charging customers extra if they ask for the WiFi password before placing their order, claiming it 'improves table turnover by 40%'.

true_false.fact: A goldfish at Bristol Aquarium has been confirmed as the oldest in captivity in the UK after celebrating its 23rd birthday last week. Staff say its secret is a 'strict diet and very calm music'.
true_false.fiction: A Scottish brewery has begun training rescue dogs to detect over-fermented kegs by scent, with the lead beagle reportedly never wrong in six months.

true_false.fact: A start-up has invented a wearable that gently vibrates to remind you to drink water — and reportedly raised £3 million in two days on Kickstarter.
true_false.fiction: Researchers at Manchester University have built an AI that can predict which biscuit you'll dunk in your tea next, based only on the way you hold the mug.

true_false.fact: A grassroots football club in the Lake District plays its home games on a pitch with a 1-in-12 slope at one end — the steepest legal gradient for organised football.
true_false.fiction: A 5-a-side league in Slough has banned all 'celebration sliding' after three players in one season tore their shorts and demanded refunds.

true_false.fact: A small Welsh railway station — Llanfair­pwllgwyngyll­gogery­chwyrn­drobwll­llanty­silio­gogogoch — sells more platform-ticket souvenirs than any other UK station.
true_false.fiction: A Norfolk B&B has started offering a 'no chit-chat' room for guests who want to skip breakfast small talk, marked with a polite door card and a £10 surcharge.

true_false.fact: The UK's bestselling biscuit in 2025 wasn't the Custard Cream or the Hobnob — it was the humble digestive, selling over 70 million packs.
true_false.fiction: A Bristol bakery has started selling 'controversial' jam doughnuts injected with mustard instead of jam, claiming a 'small but loyal' customer base.

true_false.fact: A shrimp-like creature called the mantis shrimp can throw a punch so fast it briefly boils the water around its claw, creating a flash of light. It's one of the fastest movements in the animal kingdom.
true_false.fiction: A zoo in Yorkshire has had to give its meerkats tiny sunglasses after keepers noticed they kept squinting at visitors' phone screens during photos.

true_false.fact: There's a planet-sized ball of carbon nicknamed by astronomers as a possible 'diamond' — a burnt-out star whose core may have crystallised. It's about 50 light-years from Earth.
true_false.fiction: NASA has confirmed the International Space Station now carries a small kettle, after British astronauts repeatedly complained there was 'no proper way to make a brew' in orbit.

true_false.fact: Carrots were originally purple. The familiar orange carrot was cultivated later, and is often linked to Dutch growers from around the 16th and 17th centuries.
true_false.fiction: A Cornish bakery has launched a pasty so large it legally has to be sold with its own carry-handle and a food-safety leaflet.

true_false.fact: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire. Teaching at Oxford dates back to the 11th century, while the city of Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325.
true_false.fiction: Records have revealed that a Victorian town council once employed a man whose entire job was to walk the streets and tut at people dropping litter.

true_false.fact: Hot water can freeze faster than cold water under certain conditions — an odd effect known as the Mpemba effect, still debated by scientists today.
true_false.fiction: A university in Scotland has invented an umbrella that plays a gentle warning chime thirty seconds before it's about to turn inside out in the wind.

true_false.fact: Cows have best friends and can become stressed when separated from them. Studies have shown their heart rates rise when they're kept apart from a preferred companion.
true_false.fiction: A farm in Somerset has started playing the shipping forecast to its hens after the farmer became convinced it makes them lay rounder eggs.

true_false.fact: Russia and the United States are less than 4 km apart at their closest point — two small islands in the Bering Strait known as the Diomedes.
true_false.fiction: A village in Wales has been officially recognised as having the UK's narrowest high street, where shopkeepers can shake hands across the road from their doorways.

true_false.fact: Your nose can detect roughly a trillion different smells, far more than the handful of basic categories scientists once assumed.
true_false.fiction: Doctors have identified a condition, nicknamed 'phantom buzz', where people are so used to their phone vibrating they feel it even when the phone is in another room — and it now has its own NHS leaflet.

true_false.fact: The shortest commercial flight in the world runs between two Scottish islands, Westray and Papa Westray, and can take under two minutes with a good tailwind.
true_false.fiction: A seaside town has installed Britain's first 'reverse' pier — a walkway that goes inland from the beach, after planners admitted they'd read the blueprints upside down.

true_false.fact: Bananas are slightly radioactive because they contain potassium — though you'd need to eat an impossible number in one go for it to matter at all.
true_false.fiction: A garden centre in Kent has had to rename its 'quiet corner' after customers kept falling asleep in the deckchairs and missing closing time.

true_false.fact: The Great Fire of London in 1666 destroyed thousands of houses but, remarkably, the official death toll recorded only a handful of people.
true_false.fiction: A museum has discovered that a Tudor monarch kept a 'royal sneezer' — a courtier whose sole duty was to sneeze first so the king never had to be the one who started it.

true_false.fact: Sea otters hold hands while they sleep so they don't drift apart on the water. They sometimes also wrap themselves in seaweed to stay anchored.
true_false.fiction: A wildlife park has started giving its giraffes scarves in winter, after a vet decided their long necks were 'the bit that feels the cold first'.

true_false.fact: Lightning strikes the Earth roughly 8 million times a day — about 100 times every second somewhere on the planet.
true_false.fiction: A weather station in the Lake District has had to relocate after its rain gauge kept overflowing so often that staff started using it to water the office plants.

true_false.fact: Honey is one of the only foods that effectively never spoils. Sealed pots found in ancient tombs have reportedly still been edible thousands of years later.
true_false.fiction: A chippy in Lancashire now offers a 'loyalty' batter — regulars get their initials piped onto the fish in a special edible sauce.

true_false.fact: A day on Venus is longer than its year — the planet spins so slowly that it takes longer to rotate once than to orbit the Sun.
true_false.fiction: A stargazing society in Devon has banned biscuits at meetings after too many telescopes were found with chocolatey fingerprints on the lenses.

true_false.fact: You're about one centimetre taller in the morning than at night, because the soft discs in your spine compress slightly over the course of the day.
true_false.fiction: Opticians have reported a rise in people asking for glasses with a built-in tiny wiper blade, for 'reading outdoors in the British summer'.

true_false.fact: Africa is the only continent that sits in all four hemispheres — northern, southern, eastern and western.
true_false.fiction: A town in the Midlands has installed a roundabout so confusing that the council now hands out a free laminated map to anyone approaching it for the first time.

true_false.fact: A group of flamingos is called a 'flamboyance'. They get their pink colour from the food they eat, not from birth.
true_false.fiction: A pet shop in Brighton has started offering 'taster sessions' where nervous first-time owners can borrow a goldfish for the weekend before committing.

true_false.fact: The first item ever sold on eBay, back in 1995, was reportedly a broken laser pointer — and the buyer apparently knew it was broken.
true_false.fiction: Archaeologists have found that a medieval village kept a communal cat on the payroll, paid in fish, with its own entry in the parish accounts.

true_false.fact: Some trees can 'talk' to each other through underground fungal networks, sharing nutrients and even warning signals — sometimes nicknamed the 'wood wide web'.
true_false.fiction: A National Trust garden has had to put up signs asking visitors to stop apologising to the bees, after staff noticed people muttering 'sorry' every time one flew past.

true_false.fact: The longest place name in the UK is a village on Anglesey with 58 letters — usually shortened, mercifully, to Llanfair PG.
true_false.fiction: A café in the Cotswolds holds the unofficial record for the longest-ever order, after a coach party requested 41 slightly different versions of a cup of tea.

The Eiffel Tower can grow up to 15cm taller in summer because the iron expands in the heat.
The dot above a lowercase 'i' or 'j' has a name — it's called a tittle.
Bananas are technically berries. Strawberries, somehow, are not.
Wombats produce cube-shaped poo. Scientists worked out it's the elasticity of their intestines.

Sharks existed before trees. Sharks have been around for 400 million years; trees only 350 million.
